segments.english: I have gone on at length about all this, to reconcile for you the words of Kisse Eliyahu, but my tradition I have already mentioned above. And there is proof from this that what you ask me is not from the motive of your request for the truth, as you said, but rather to seek some pretext. And who am I that you should hold me to be a Kabbalist, for I am brutish and do not know. And all my prayers are not even like the chirping of birds, for the birds are fed without distress, and on them there lies neither the yoke of kingship nor the yoke of worldly occupation, and chirping can be done with intent, but I, under so much burden of the times and the cares of livelihood, have my mind and my thoughts confused. And furthermore, I have not received from a wise Kabbalist mouth to mouth. Would that the LORD relieve me of the troubles of time and of livelihood, and provide me a Kabbalist master who would set me on the paths of uprightness, and that I might merit to be among the sons of ascent. As for what I answered you the second time, it is the words of Kisse Eliyahu that you turned a blind eye to. And as for what you wrote, that you do not ascribe corporeality to the sefirot, but did you not write: "If so, there would be a force in a body"? And this time you say that light is a subtle body. And I already wrote to you that what they called them by the name light is only in order to accommodate the ear; one time you ascribe corporeality and another time you make excuses. And why do all these doubts come into your mind, except because you ascribe corporeality? As for what you wrote: "Who is it that governs all these hidden worlds?" The one who brings them into being is the one who keeps them alive. And as for what you wrote, that Ze'ir Anpin is found to be the god of the lower ones. Have I not written to you that he is nothing but a tool for the acts of the Creator? And as for what you wrote, that some of them said "all the great work of the LORD," from which it follows that there is a small one? Those who say so have themselves already explained that they meant Metatron, whose name is like his master's, as they said in the Talmud: "And to Moses He said, 'Come up to the LORD'; it should have said 'to Me'. But this is Metatron, whose name is like his master's"; and so it is in the Yalkut. And as for what you wrote, that our true rabbis said, it is cited in Menorat ha-Ma'or that at the time of the giving of the Torah the Holy One, blessed be He, tore 7 heavens, etc. And in Midrash Rabbah they said: "I am the LORD your God; I am the first and I am the last. I am the first, for I have no father, and I am the last, for I have no son; and besides Me there is no God, for I have no brother." Who is it that says he has a father, or a son, or a brother? Rather, you spread slander against the sages who say so, and they have already explained their words, of blessed memory, that all the epithets and the attributes are in the sefirot, to accommodate the ear. Go now and see what Mahari Gikatilia wrote in the introduction to Sha'arei Orah, and the divine Rabbi Menachem Rikanti, and Rabbi Y. Chayyim, and these are his words: "In sum, wherever you see things that are not fitting to say of the Creator, may He be blessed, such as measure of stature and the like, it is all said of the sefirot; and when you see them speak in the manner of praise and thanksgiving, it is all said of the Creator, may He be blessed, who is within them and outside them, for nothing limits Him; therefore one may not say of the Creator, may He be blessed, not right and not left, not face and not back, etc." See there. And as for what you wrote, that the opinion of the Kabbalists is that the sefirot descend in a chain, by nature like a son from the father, far be it that they said so. On the contrary, they said: "Far be it to believe or to bring to mind that the sefirot are part of Ein Sof that came out of it and descended from cause to effect, for it is a criminal sin. For Ein Sof is not divided into parts, God forbid, and it receives no addition and no diminution, but its existence is constant always, without any change whatever, and He originated them, an absolute origination."

tokens.gloss: I have gone on at length

tokens.note: לישב (ליישב): literally 'to settle'; said of a difficult passage it means to resolve or reconcile it.
Kisse Eliyahu: 'the Throne of Elijah', the literal sense of the title; the abbreviation כס"א is written out.
קבלתי: from קבלה, the received tradition, with the first-person suffix: 'my tradition', which the writer says he has already mentioned above. The verb 'I received' is also possible; see readings.
Ps 73:22 ('I am brutish'); see apparatus.
תפלותי: 'my prayers' (תפלות, plural of תפלה, written without the yod). The same consonants could mean 'my foolishness'; see readings.
דרך ארץ, literally 'the way of the land': worldly occupation, earning a living. The pair 'the yoke of kingship and the yoke of worldly occupation' is the Mishnah's wording.
The root of 'Kabbalah'. Here 'I have received': the writer has not had the tradition from a master.
A Kabbalist: one who holds the received tradition.

'sons of ascent' (בני עליה): a Talmudic phrase for the elevated, those few who have risen to a high spiritual rank; the writer hopes to be among them. The old note ('a higher stage of learning') narrows it.
'if so' (אם כן).
'light': the name the Kabbalists give the sefirot; the writer argues that it is used as a name, not as a thing.
'in order': the purpose of the name, as the writer gives it.

לשבר את האזן, literally 'to break the ear': to make a matter fit what the hearer can take in. It is the Kabbalists' reason for speaking of God in physical terms, and it is the writer's answer to the charge of corporeality.
The idiom לשבר את האזן, 'to break the ear' = 'to accommodate the ear'; the same at 2:29.301-303.
'at one time' and 'another time' (פעם ... ופעם): the writer's point that the reader alternates between two errors.

tokens.gloss: the one who brings into being

tokens.note: Ze'ir Anpin: Aramaic 'small face', the name of a partzuf (ז"א = Ze'ir Anpin).
'god of': the questioner's charge, in his words. The Hebrew is 'elohei' (god of the lower ones).
the LORD: the Tetragrammaton in the quoted verse, Deut 11:7.
Metatron: the name as the Talmud gives it.
the LORD: in Exod 24:1.
'to Me' (אלי): the Talmud's point that the verse should have said 'to Me' and does not.
וכ"ה = וכן הוא, 'and so it is'.
Yalkut: a Midrash anthology. The title is transliterated; its sense is 'compilation'.
Menorat ha-Ma'or: 'the candelabrum of the light'. The title is transliterated; the meaning is given here.

tokens.gloss: the Holy One, blessed be He
tokens.note: the Holy One, blessed be He (הקב"ה).
the LORD: Exod 20:2 ('I am the LORD your God'), as quoted in the Midrash.
God: Isa 44:6 ('besides Me there is no God'), in the Midrash quotation.
The printed word is 'בם' ('in them'). Read as 'son' (בן) from the sense of the list; see apparatus.
'of blessed memory' (ז"ל).
Literally 'to break the ear': to make a matter fit what the hearer can take in. The same idiom as at 2:29.143-145.
Mahari: 'our teacher, the Rav Rabbi Y.' (morenu ha-Rav Rabbi Y.). The first name is not given in the text.
Sha'arei Orah: 'Gates of Light'. The title is transliterated.
'the divine' (האלהי): the honorific before the name, kept as written; it is not a claim about the man.
ר"מ: the initial M. is expanded from the surname: Menachem Recanati, the Italian Kabbalist, is meant. The text gives only the initial.
ר"י חיים: only the initial Y. and the surname Chayyim are given; no expansion is certain, so the initial stays.
'and these are his words': the formula that opens the quotation.
'In sum' (סוף דבר: literally 'the end of the matter').
may He be blessed (ית').
שיעור קומה, 'the measure of the stature': the title of the early mystical text that describes the dimensions of the Divine Body; the writer uses it as an example of such language.
may He be blessed (ית').
may He be blessed (ית').
'etc.': the quotation is cut short in the text.
'see there' (עיין שם).
descend in a chain: the chain of descent (השתלשלות), here as the verb.
Ein Sof: literally 'without end'. It is used as a name with no article.
'descended': the verb of the chain of descent.
'cause' (עילה).
'effect' (עלול).
'criminal' (פלילי): a sin for which one is judged, a legal term.
The ש opens a sentence after a full stop; the English supplies 'For' and keeps the main clause.
'God forbid' (ח"ו).
'originated': renewed, created anew. The writer's word for the origin of the sefirot.

grammar: The paragraph is the respondent's reply to his questioner, in the respondent's own voice. 'You' is the questioner, and the English keeps the second person.

Each point of the questioner's letter is answered in turn, opening with 'as for what you wrote' (2:29.101, 112, 160, 173, 187, 230, 373). The questions with 'but did you not' and 'and why' keep their force as questions.

Clauses with 'that' after 'you wrote' are reported speech and take no quotation marks. 'You wrote: if so ...' and 'you wrote: who is it ...' quote the questioner's own words, so they are in quotation marks.

The Talmud passage turns on the word 'to Me' (אלי): the verse should have said 'to Me', and the Talmud draws its conclusion from the difference. The English gives the Hebrew point in single quotation marks inside the double ones. 'אלי מבעי ליה' is Aramaic in the Talmud's wording; מכלל דאיכא קטן is Aramaic too.
The verb 'to ascribe corporeality' (להגשים) and its forms run through the paragraph. It is the error the writer charges against the questioner, and it is rendered the same way each time.

The idiom לשבר את האזן (2:29.143-145, 301-303), 'to break the ear', means to accommodate the ear, that is, to bring a matter within what the hearer can take in. The respondent uses it twice for the Kabbalists' physical epithets.
segments.note: The respondent's reply (2:29) in the respondent's voice. Honorifics, book titles and abbreviations are rendered by the decisions for this work; see the notes at the first occurrence of each.
apparatus: Witness: Wikisource base text. The 1931 scan is not yet collated, so the text is translated as read and this is flagged here (decisions, Q2).

Bible verses: Exod 20:2 ('I am the LORD your God', 2:29.249-251, in the Midrash quotation); Isa 44:6 ('I am the first and I am the last, and besides Me there is no God', 2:29.252-271); Exod 24:1 ('And to Moses He said: Come up to the LORD', 2:29.213-218, in the Talmud quotation); Deut 11:7 ('all the great work of the LORD', 2:29.191-194); Ps 73:22 ('I am brutish and do not know', 2:29.38-40); Prov 4:11 ('the paths of uprightness', 2:29.95-96).
Variant: the printed 'בם' (2:29.279), 'in them'. Read as 'בן' (son), the likelier word in 'a father or a son or a brother'. The printed word is kept in the Hebrew; the English follows the sense.
The Talmud and Midrash passages carry no reference in the text, and none is added.
The quotation 'In sum ...' ends at 2:29.371 and is followed by 'See there' (2:29.372). The quotation 'Far be it ...' closes at 2:29.430.
Bible allusions: 'a criminal sin' (2:29.406-407) is Job 31:28 ('this too is a criminal sin'; cf. 31:11); 'spread slander' (2:29.284-285) is Num 14:36 ('and they spread slander') and Prov 10:18.

readings.note: קבלתי as a verb: 'but I received, I already mentioned it above'; the English takes the noun 'my tradition'.
תפלות 'foolishness' has the same consonants; the English takes 'prayers' from the context.
The printed בם is 'in them'; the English reads the likelier בן, 'son'.
